text: Hamilton: An American Musical is a sung-and-rapped-through biographical musical with music, lyrics, and a book by Lin-Manuel Miranda, based on the 2004 biography Alexander Hamilton by Ron Chernow. The musical chronicles the life of American Founding Father Alexander Hamilton, detailing his role in the American Revolution and early U.S. political history. Composed from 2008 to 2015, its music draws heavily from hip hop, as well as R&B, pop, soul, and traditional-style show tunes. It casts non-white actors as the Founding Fathers and other historical figures. Miranda described the musical as about "America then, as told by America now." The show received near-universal acclaim upon its opening off-Broadway on February 17, 2015, at the Public Theater in Lower Manhattan, where Miranda played Alexander Hamilton and the engagement was sold out. It won eight Drama Desk Awards, including Outstanding Musical, and transferred to the Richard Rodgers Theatre on Broadway, opening on August 6, 2015, receiving positive reviews and strong box office performance. At the 70th Tony Awards, it received 16 nominations and won 11 awards, including Best Musical, and was awarded the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. A filmed version of the Broadway production was released on Disney+ in 2020, followed by a theatrical release in 2025 by Walt Disney Pictures. The Chicago production began preview performances at the CIBC Theatre in September 2016 and opened the following month. The West End production opened at the Victoria Palace Theatre in London on December 21, 2017, after previews from December 6, and won seven Olivier Awards in 2018, including Best New Musical. The first U.S. national tour began in March 2017, a second U.S. tour opened in February 2018, and the third U.S. tour began on January 11, 2019, with a three-week engagement in Puerto Rico where Miranda returned to play Hamilton. The first non-English production opened in Hamburg in October 2022, translated into German. As of 2025, no amateur or professional licenses have been granted for Hamilton. The musical is structured in two acts and covers Hamilton's early life as an orphan on the island of St. Croix, his immigration to New York City, his meeting with Aaron Burr, John Laurens, the Marquis de Lafayette, and Hercules Mulligan at King's College in 1776, and his involvement in the Revolutionary War as George Washington's aide-de-camp. It details his marriage to Eliza Schuyler, his career as a lawyer and Secretary of the Treasury, and his complex relationship with Aaron Burr, culminating in their duel that ends Hamilton's life. At a ball hosted by Philip Schuyler, Eliza falls in love with Hamilton, who reciprocates, leading to their marriage ("Helpless"), while Angelica suppresses her own feelings ("Satisfied"). After the wedding, Burr and Hamilton celebrate their successes ("The Story of Tonight (Reprise)"), with Burr reflecting on Hamilton's rapid rise and his own affair with Theodosia. During the Battle of Monmouth, Hamilton aids Laurens in a duel against Major General Charles Lee ("Ten Duel Commandments"), resulting in Washington suspending him ("Meet Me Inside"). Eliza reveals she is pregnant with their first child, Philip, and urges Hamilton to slow down ("That Would Be Enough"). Lafayette convinces Washington to recall Hamilton for field command at the Battle of Yorktown ("Guns and Ships"), and Washington tells him that his actions will be remembered forever ("History Has Its Eyes on You"). At Yorktown, Hamilton works with Lafayette to defeat the British and uncovers Mulligan's espionage ("Yorktown (The World Turned Upside Down)"). After Yorktown, King George III questions the new nation's ability to survive ("What Comes Next?"). Hamilton's son Philip is born, and Burr has a daughter, Theodosia, with the two fathers promising to protect their children ("Dear Theodosia"). After Laurens is killed in a post-war battle, Hamilton grieves and redoubles his work ("Tomorrow There'll Be More of Us (The Laurens Interlude)"). Over the next decade, both Hamilton and Burr work as lawyers, with Hamilton gaining influence, participating in the Constitutional Convention, co-authoring The Federalist Papers, and becoming Secretary of the Treasury under President Washington, while Eliza urges him to slow down and Angelica moves to London. In 1789, Thomas Jefferson returns from France as Secretary of State ("What'd I Miss"), and Jefferson and James Madison debate Hamilton's financial plans at a Cabinet meeting ("Cabinet Battle #1"). Washington orders Hamilton to find a compromise, which he achieves through a private dinner, resulting in Hamilton's financial plan being passed in exchange for the permanent capital being placed on the Potomac River. Burr is envious of Hamilton's power and defeats Hamilton's father-in-law Philip Schuyler in a Senate race ("Schuyler Defeated"). In a second Cabinet meeting, Hamilton argues for U.S. neutrality during France's conflict with Britain, which Washington supports ("Cabinet Battle #2"). Jefferson, Madison, and Burr then unite to discredit Hamilton ("Washington on Your Side"). After Washington retires, Hamilton helps write his farewell address ("One Last Time"). King George learns of Washington's departure and is replaced by John Adams ("I Know Him"), who fires Hamilton, prompting Hamilton to publish a critical critique of Adams ("The Adams Administration"). Jefferson, Madison, and Burr confront Hamilton about James Reynolds's blackmail, accusing him of embezzlement ("We Know"). To defend himself, Hamilton recalls his life and the role writing has played in saving him ("Hurricane"), then publicly releases the Reynolds Pamphlet, damaging his reputation ("The Reynolds Pamphlet") and destroying his relationship with Eliza, who burns all his letters to erase herself from history ("Burn"). At 19, Hamilton's son Philip duels George Eacker ("Blow Us All Away") and is fatally shot ("Stay Alive (Reprise)"), leading to reconciliation between Alexander and Eliza ("It's Quiet Uptown"). Hamilton's endorsement of Jefferson over Burr in the 1800 presidential election ("The Election of 1800") deepens the rivalry, prompting Burr to challenge Hamilton to a duel via letter exchange ("Your Obedient Servant"). Hamilton writes his final letter while Eliza tells him to go to bed ("Best of Wives and Best of Women"). Burr reflects on the events leading to the duel, while Hamilton reflects on his legacy before throwing away his shot. Burr fatally shoots Hamilton, lamenting that though he survives, he is remembered as the villain who killed Hamilton ("The World Was Wide Enough"). The musical closes with a reflection on historical memory, as Jefferson and Madison reflect on Hamilton's legacy, and Eliza recounts how she reinserted herself into history by recording veterans' memories, raising funds for the Washington Monument, speaking out against slavery, and establishing the first private orphanage in New York City ("Who Lives, Who Dies, Who Tells Your Story"). Eliza then turns to the audience and lets out a tearful gasp. The original Broadway cast recording was made available by NPR on September 21, 2015, released digitally by Atlantic Records on September 25, 2015, and physically on October 16, 2015, with a vinyl release following. The album debuted at number 12 on the Billboard 200, the highest entrance for a cast recording since 1963, reached number 2 on the Billboard 200, and number 1 on the Billboard Rap albums chart. It won a Grammy Award for Best Musical Theater Album. The Hamilton Mixtape, a collection of remixes, covers, and samples, was released on December 2, 2016, and debuted at number 1 on the Billboard 200. The Hamilton Instrumentals, an instrumental version of the original cast recording, was released on June 30, 2017. Producers announced free sing-along programs and authorized the use of the Hamiltunes name and logo for fan events, which had already occurred in Los Angeles, San Francisco, Washington D.C., and elsewhere. Miranda launched a series of 13 Hamilton-related recordings called Hamildrops, released monthly from December 2017 to December 2018. The first, "Ben Franklin's Song" by The Decemberists, released on December 15, 2017, contains lyrics Miranda wrote for an unused song, imagined as Benjamin Franklin singing in a "Decemberist-y way." The second, "Wrote My Way Out (Remix)," released on January 25, 2018, is a remixed version of a song from The Hamilton Mixtape featuring Royce Da 5'9", Joyner Lucas, Black Thought, and Aloe Blacc. The third, "The Hamilton Polka" by "Weird Al" Yankovic, released on March 2, 2018, is a polka medley of musical songs, with Yankovic jokingly calling March 2 "February 30th" due to his scheduling. After the show premiered on Disney+ in July 2020, Yankovic released a video version of the song synced to clips from the show. The fourth, "Found/Tonight," released on March 19, 2018, is a mash-up of "You Will Be Found" from Dear Evan Hansen and "The Story of Tonight," with proceeds benefiting the March for Our Lives initiative. The fifth, "First Burn," released on April 30, 2018, features five actresses who played Eliza: Arianna Afsar, Julia Harriman, Shoba Narayan, Rachelle Ann Go, and Lexi Lawson, and is the first draft of "Burn," with Miranda noting the original version was angrier and more reactive, while the final version gives Eliza agency. The sixth, a cover of "Helpless" by The Regrettes, released on May 31, 2018, was suggested by producer Mike Elizondo. The seventh, "Boom Goes the Cannon..." by Mobb Deep, released on June 18, 2018, samples "Right Hand Man" and was one of the last recordings by Havoc and Prodigy before Prodigy's death in June 2017; Havoc dedicated it to Queensbridge. The eighth, "Rise Up, Wise Up, Eyes Up" by Ibeyi, was released on August 31, 2018. The ninth, "A Forgotten Spot (Olvidado)," released on September 20, 2018, features Puerto Rican artists Zion & Lennox, De La Ghetto, Ivy Queen, PJ Sin Suela, and Lucecita Benítez, and was created to mark the one-year anniversary of Hurricane Maria. The tenth, a rendition of "Theodosia Reprise" by Sara Bareilles, released on Halloween 2018, features Alex Lacamoire on piano and Questlove of The Roots on drums and was originally intended for Act 2 but cut from the final production. The eleventh, "Cheering For Me Now," released on November 20, 2018, is an original song based on the 1788 Federal Procession in New York City, with Miranda performing as Hamilton and arranged by Alex Lacamoire. The final release, "One Last Time (44 Remix)," released on December 20, 2018, features Christopher Jackson (George Washington), BeBe Winans, and Barack Obama (reciting lines from Washington's farewell address), with the "44" referencing Obama as the 44th U.S. president. The Broadway show's orchestration includes the conductor playing the first keyboard part. While on vacation from In the Heights, Lin-Manuel Miranda read the 2004 biography Alexander Hamilton by Ron Chernow and began envisioning a musical, finding only a 1917 Broadway play starring George Arliss as Hamilton. Miranda began a project titled The Hamilton Mixtape, and on May 12, 2009, performed the first song from it at a White House event.

The musical *Hamilton* is based on lines from George Washington's farewell address and features a gospel-style arrangement of the song "One Last Time," with the number "44" in the title signifying that Barack Obama was the 44th president of the United States. Lin-Manuel Miranda, while on vacation from performing in his Broadway show *In the Heights*, read Ron Chernow’s 2004 biography *Alexander Hamilton* and began envisioning a stage musical about Hamilton’s life, discovering that a play on Hamilton had previously been performed on Broadway in 1917 starring George Arliss. Miranda developed a project called *The Hamilton Mixtape*, and on May 12, 2009, he performed an early version of "Alexander Hamilton" at the White House Evening of Poetry, Music and the Spoken Word. He later worked on "My Shot" over the next year. The musical’s story and lyrics are heavily researched, with many songs drawing directly from primary sources such as personal letters, The Federalist Papers, and the Reynolds Pamphlet, and Miranda has cited *The West Wing* as an influence. A workshop production titled *The Hamilton Mixtape* was held at Vassar College and the New York Stage and Film Powerhouse Theater on July 27, 2013, directed by Thomas Kail and musically directed by Alex Lacamoire, featuring Miranda as Hamilton, Utkarsh Ambudkar as Burr, Christopher Jackson as Washington, Daveed Diggs as Lafayette/Jefferson, Ana Nogueira as Eliza, Anika Noni Rose as Angelica, Javier Muñoz as Laurens, Presilah Nunez as Peggy/Maria, and Joshua Henry as Mulligan/Madison/King George. Only Miranda, Diggs, and Jackson from that cast joined the off-Broadway production; Ambudkar was replaced due to alcoholism, and Brian d'Arcy James was replaced by Jonathan Groff as King George III. A 2014 workshop at the 52nd Street Project included Miranda as Hamilton, Leslie Odom Jr. as Burr, Diggs as Lafayette/Jefferson, Phillipa Soo as Eliza, Renée Elise Goldsberry as Angelica, Anthony Ramos as Laurens/Philip, Okieriete Onaodowan as Mulligan/Madison, Ciara Renée as Peggy/Maria, James as King George III, and Isaiah Johnson as Washington, with an audio recording available on YouTube. Directed by Thomas Kail and choreographed by Andy Blankenbuehler, the musical premiered Off-Broadway at The Public Theater on January 20, 2015, with previews and an official opening on February 17, extended to April 5 and then to May 3, with Ron Chernow serving as historical consultant. It opened to universal acclaim and won 11 Tony Awards. Producer Jeffrey Seller wanted to move the show to Broadway before the end of the 2014–2015 season to qualify for the Tony Awards, but Miranda and Kail overruled him, wanting more time. Changes between off-Broadway and Broadway included cutting several numbers, rewriting Hamilton’s final moments, and shortening "One Last Ride" to "One Last Time" to focus on Washington’s decision not to seek a third term. The show premiered on Broadway at the Richard Rodgers Theatre on July 13, 2015, in previews and opened on August 6, 2015, produced by Seller, Jill Furman, and Sandy Jacobs, with sets by David Korins, costumes by Paul Tazewell, lighting by Howell Binkley, and sound by Nevin Steinberg. In April 2016, the cast reached a profit-sharing agreement with producers, an uncommon arrangement. The show suspended production on March 12, 2020, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, resuming on September 14, 2021. It began previews at the CIBC Theatre in Chicago on September 27, 2016, with Miguel Cervantes as Hamilton, Joshua Henry as Burr, Karen Olivo as Angelica, Arianna Afsar as Eliza, Alexander Gemignani as King George III, Jonathan Kirkland as Washington, and Samantha Marie Ware as Peggy/Maria, receiving positive reviews on opening in October and closing on January 5, 2020, after 1,341 shows and grossing $400 million, with over 2.6 million attendees including 31,000 public school students through the Hamilton Education Program. Plans for a national tour emerged in January 2016, initially with over 20 stops from 2017 through 2020; tickets for the San Francisco debut sold out within 24 hours, with over 110,000 people entering the waiting room. The first tour began previews at the SHN Orpheum Theatre on March 10, 2017, officially opening on March 23, running in San Francisco until August 5, then transferring to Los Angeles’s Hollywood Pantages Theatre from August 11 to December 30, 2017. A second U.S. tour, the "Philip Tour," began previews at the Paramount Theatre in Seattle on February 6, 2018, officially opening on February 15, 2018. The "Angelica Tour" required 14 truckloads and over 60 traveling cast, crew, and musicians, with two portable sets built for each tour to allow for advance assembly. The Philip Tour premiered in Canada at the Ed Mirvish Theatre in Toronto on February 11, 2020, scheduled to run until May 17, but was canceled from March 14 due to the pandemic. The Angelica Tour concluded on June 25, 2023, at the Centro de Bellas Artes Luis A. Ferré in Puerto Rico, and re-opened on September 4, 2024, at the Hollywood Pantages Theatre alongside the Philip Tour. A third touring company, the "And Peggy Tour," was announced on November 8, 2017, to debut in January 2019 at the University of Puerto Rico’s Teatro UPR in San Juan, with Miranda reprising the title role, later moving to San Francisco. Due to union concerns over budget cuts, the engagement was moved to the Luis A. Ferré Performing Arts Center and shortened to January 11–27, 2019, with police standing outside on opening night. Miranda’s performance at the venue marked his return nine years after playing Usnavi in *In the Heights*. The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon taped segments in Puerto Rico, with Miranda and Fallon performing a version of "The Story of Tonight" ending with a salsa rendition of the show’s opening. In a review, Chris Jones noted Miranda’s deeper emotions, improved vocal and dance technique, and praised Donald Webber Jr.’s performance as Burr; the three-week run raised about $15 million for Miranda’s Flamboyán Arts Fund, including funding for Teatro UPR’s restoration. A filmed version of "Alexander Hamilton" from the Puerto Rico production was shown as the final part of *Hamilton: The Exhibition* in 2019. Julius Thomas III took over the role of Hamilton when the And Peggy Tour moved to San Francisco, opening on February 21, 2019, and was fixed in San Francisco with no traveling dates, closing on March 11, 2020, due to the pandemic, reopening on August 10, 2021, and closing on September 5, 2021, with its final performance in Toronto on August 20, 2023. A planned Los Angeles production from March 12 to November 22, 2020, was suspended due to the pandemic and later opened on August 27, 2021, running until March 20, 2022, named the Eliza Tour. Cameron Mackintosh produced a London production that reopened the Victoria Palace Theatre on December 21, 2017, after previews from December 6, receiving positive reviews; Prince Harry attended a charity performance in 2018, singing a few bars of "You'll Be Back" as King George III. The London production closed on March 16, 2020, due to the pandemic, announced to reopen in 2021, and reopened on August 19, 2021. The Australian premiere began at Sydney Lyric on March 17, 2021, with Jason Arrow as Hamilton, Chloé Zuel as Eliza, Lyndon Watts as Burr, Akina Edmonds as Angelica, Matu Ngaropo as Washington, Victory Ndukwe as Lafayette/Jefferson, Shaka Cook as Mulligan/Madison, Marty Alix as Laurens/Philip, Elandrah Eramiha as Peggy/Maria, and Brent Hill as King George III, suspended on June 25, 2021, and resuming on October 19. The production opened in Melbourne at Her Majesty’s Theatre on March 15, 2022, with a Ham4Ham show on March 22, and received positive reviews, with Jason Arrow praised and Standby Tigist Strode receiving acclaim; Sami Afuni took over Mulligan/Madison and Rowan Witt joined as King George, ending the season on January 15, 2023. The Australian tour continued in Brisbane at the Lyric Theatre, QPAC from January 2023, concluding on April 23. Stage Entertainment announced a German production in 2019 to open at the Operettenhaus in Hamburg, originally scheduled for November 2021, postponed due to the pandemic, with previews starting September 24, 2022, and opening on October 6, 2022, becoming the first non-English production, with lyrics translated by Kevin Schroeder and Sera Finale. The German production ended in October 2023 after one year due to poor ticket sales. The Australian producers announced an international tour to begin in Auckland, New Zealand at Spark Arena in May 2023, featuring the Australian cast and being the first staged in an arena. On March 28, 2023, Miranda announced the musical’s Asian premiere in Manila, Philippines, in September at the Solaire Resort & Casino, with previews starting September 21, 2023, and opening on November 11, 2023, featuring Australian cast members including Jason Arrow as Hamilton and Filipino actress Rachelle Ann Go as Eliza; the production ran until November 26, 2023, then moved to Abu Dhabi in 2024, running from January 17 to February 11 at the Etihad Arena.

The Australian producers, Michael Cassel Group, announced an international tour beginning in Auckland, New Zealand at Spark Arena in May 2023, featuring the Australian cast and marking the first arena staging of the production. On March 28, 2023, through GMG Productions' social media, Miranda announced the musical's Asian premiere in Manila, Philippines, at the Solaire Resort & Casino's theatre in September 2023, with previews starting on September 21 and opening night on November 11, 2023. Several Australian cast members, including Jason Arrow as Alexander Hamilton, returned for the first Asian production, which ran until November 26, 2023. Filipino actress Rachelle Ann Go reprised her role as Eliza from the original West End production. After Manila, the show moved to Abu Dhabi in 2024, running from January 17 to February 11 at the Etihad Arena, before transferring to Singapore on April 19 at the Sands Theatre, Marina Bay Sands. A UK and Ireland tour began at the Palace Theatre, Manchester on November 11, 2023, and toured to Edinburgh, Bristol, Birmingham, Dublin, Cardiff, Bradford, Southampton, Liverpool, Sunderland, Plymouth, and Norwich, with the full cast announced on September 21, including Shaq Taylor in the titular role. Hamilton's off-Broadway engagement at The Public Theater was sold out, and when it opened on Broadway, it had a multimillion-dollar advance, reportedly earning $30 million before opening. By September 2015, the show was sold out for most of its Broadway run and was the second-highest-grossing show on Broadway during the Labor Day week ending September 6, 2015, behind only The Lion King. In late November 2016, Hamilton set a Broadway box office record by grossing $3.3 million in a single eight-performance week, becoming the first show to exceed $3 million in eight performances. The musical offers a ticket lottery before each show, initially with 21 front-row seats and occasional standing room tickets; Hamilton creator Lin-Manuel Miranda began hosting outdoor mini-performances, called "Ham4Ham," before each daily drawing, allowing lottery participants to experience parts of the show and giving winners the chance to purchase two tickets for the price of one ($10 bill). HowlRound characterized Ham4Ham as part of a tradition of Latina/o theatremaking, emphasizing accessibility and social media engagement, noting it aligns with the philosophy of "taking the theatre to the people." The Ham4Ham shows drew unusually large crowds, causing congestion on West 46th Street, leading to an online ticket lottery beginning in early January 2016, which on its first day saw over 50,000 entries that crashed the website. After Miranda left the show on July 9, 2016, Rory O'Malley, who played King George III, took over as host of Ham4Ham, which officially ended on August 31, 2016. The online lottery continued, with a mobile app released in August 2017 that expanded the lottery to include touring productions and the Broadway show. Marilyn Stasio of Variety praised the off-Broadway production, noting the music was exhilarating and the lyrics were a surprise, with each character's singing style tailored to their persona, and that Miranda's narrative became a collective story of a nation built by immigrants. Jesse Green of New York highlighted the show's method of exploring the conflict between independence and interdependence, noting the references to Rodgers and Hammerstein, Gilbert and Sullivan, Sondheim, West Side Story, and 1776, as well as the excellence of the duels, which were handled superbly by director Thomas Kail and choreographer Andy Blankenbuehler. Elisabeth Vincentelli of the New York Post, which was founded by Hamilton's creator, criticized the show's portrayal of Hamilton and Burr's relationship, stating it fails to drive the narrative and that many numbers are exposition-heavy, especially those involving George Washington. Ben Brantley of The New York Times described the Broadway production as worth seeing, noting the characters' costumes and the set's period-appropriate tavern atmosphere. David Cote of Time Out New York called Hamilton a sublime blend of hip-hop, R&B, Britpop, and traditional showstoppers, praising its human drama and novelistic density, and named it a Critics' Pick with five stars. Andrew Schocket of the Journal of the Early Republic noted that while Hamilton strays from the "American Revolution Rebooted" genre, it remains rooted in it, and Marvin McAllister observed that the hip-hop influence works well because Miranda elevates the form through musical theater storytelling, ennobling both the culture and its creators. The Economist described the show's critical reception as "near-universal acclaim," and Barack Obama joked in 2016 that admiration for the musical is the only thing he and Dick Cheney agree on. In 2019, The Guardian ranked Hamilton the second-greatest theatrical work since 2000. Some feminist scholars have criticized the show for its depiction of women, with theatre professor Stacy Wolf noting that female characters are assigned limited and stereotypical roles, and musicologist Cheryl L. Keyes arguing that Eliza, Angelica, and Maria Reynolds conform to the "good wife," "gold digger," and "whore" tropes found in hip-hop. Andy Blankenbuehler received a Special Drama Desk Award for his choreography, which is described as "inspired and heart-stopping" and "indispensable" to the storytelling. The musical holds the record for most Tony Award nominations with 16 (though due to multiple actor nominations, it could have won only 13 unless a tie occurred), eventually winning 11 awards, the second-most ever for a single production, behind The Producers (2001), which won twelve. The New Yorker described the show as an achievement of historical and cultural reimagining, noting the costumes and set reflect the period with velvet frock coats and knee britches, a wooden scaffold against exposed brick, and warm lighting suggesting candlelight. The musical is mostly sung and rapped throughout, with little dialogue outside the score. Miranda stated that the portrayal of Hamilton, Jefferson, Washington, and other white historical figures by Black, Latino, and Asian actors does not require suspension of disbelief, saying the cast reflects how America looks now, allowing audiences to leave cultural baggage about the founding fathers at the door and making the story more immediate and accessible. The show emphasizes Hamilton's immigrant status, highlighting his work ethic and intelligence, and promotes a pro-immigration message by portraying him as an immigrant who "gets the job done," thus fostering a positive image of immigrants and illustrating America's complex racial history and identity. Renee Elise Goldsberry, who played Angelica Schuyler, said the show is a story about America told by a diverse cast with diverse musical styles, offering the opportunity to reclaim a history some feel is not theirs. Miranda has stated he is "totally open" to women playing the Founding Fathers, and the British production featured predominantly Black British artists. Although based on historical events, Miranda used dramatic license in retelling the story. Critics have pointed out a simplistic portrayal of Hamilton and a vilification of Jefferson; Joanne B. Freeman of Yale noted that real Hamilton was a contradictory figure who distrusted immigrants and valued law and order. Australian historian Shane White found the framing of the story "troubling," stating it centers on the Founding Fathers rather than including ordinary people, African-Americans, Native Americans, and women in a more inclusive narrative. Rutgers University professor Lyra Monteiro criticized the multi-ethnic casting for obscuring the absence of identifiable enslaved or free persons of color, and noted other commentators, such as Ishmael Reed, argued the show makes Hamilton and others appear more progressive on racial justice than they were. Policy analyst Matt Stoller criticized the musical's portrayal of Hamilton as an idealist, contrasting it with the historical record of Hamilton's reactionary, anti-democratic politics, citing his role in the Newburgh conspiracy, development of a financial system that empowered the wealthy, and use of military force, indefinite detention, and mass arrests during the Whiskey Rebellion. In 2018, Historians on Hamilton: How a Blockbuster Musical Is Restaging America's Past was published, with fifteen historians analyzing how the musical engages with and misinterprets history. Theatre scholars Meredith Conti and Meron Langsner have published analyses of firearms and dueling in the musical. Ishmael Reed wrote and produced the 2019 play The Haunting of Lin-Manuel Miranda, which critiques Hamilton's historical inaccuracies, initially running at Nuyorican Poets Cafe in May 2019 and again in October 2019. Philosopher Michael Sandel critiques Hamilton for oversimplistic multiculturalism, avoiding discussions on Hamilton's financial doctrines, and embracing liberal meritocracy in his 2022 edition of Democracy's Discontent. KQED News reported that a growing number of U.S. history teachers are using the Hamilton phenomenon to inspire students, with Cabinet rap battles engaging students on traditionally uninteresting topics. An elective course on Hamilton was offered at Ethical Culture Fieldston School in New York, and KQED noted that the show is especially galvanizing for students who find 18th-century America distant and irrelevant, as it presents the Founding Fathers as real humans with feelings and flaws, not as "bloodless, two-dimensional cutouts." A Bronx teacher noted his students were singing the songs like they would sing the latest releases from Drake or Adele, and one teacher emphasized Hamilton's ability to write his way out of trouble as a sign of scholarship and upward mobility. Hamilton's producers pledged to provide 20,000 New York City public high school students from low-income families with subsidized tickets at $70, with the Rockefeller Foundation contributing $1.5 million to reduce prices to $10 per student. The Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History created a study guide to accompany the student-ticket program. Through a private grant, nearly 20,000 Chicago Public Schools students saw a special performance in 2017, with some performing original songs on stage. EducationWorld praised the musical for revitalizing interest in civic education, and Northwestern University announced plans in 2017 to offer coursework in history, Latino studies, and interdisciplinary studies inspired by Hamilton. In 2016, Moraine Valley Community College launched the "Straight Outta Hamilton" movement, hosting panels and events connecting the musical to current events. In 2015, the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced a redesign of the $10 bill, with plans to replace Hamilton with a then-undecided woman from American history.

The Hamilton Education Program, founded in 2016 with funding from the Rockefeller Foundation, is a collaboration between the producers of Hamilton, the Miranda Family, and the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History. It established the Ham4Progress Award for Educational Advancement to support college-bound high school juniors from communities affected by social injustice or discrimination. The Gilder Lehrman Institute also created a study guide to accompany the student-ticket program, which aimed to lower ticket prices to $10 per student. Through a private grant, nearly 20,000 Chicago Public Schools students saw a special performance of the show in 2017, with some performing original songs on stage. The website EducationWorld praised Hamilton for revitalizing interest in civic education, and Northwestern University announced plans in 2017 to offer coursework inspired by the musical in history, Latino studies, and interdisciplinary studies. Moraine Valley Community College launched a Hamilton appreciation movement, Straight Outta Hamilton, hosting panels and events linking the musical to current events. In 2015, the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced a redesign of the $10 bill to feature a woman from American history, but due to Hamilton's rising popularity, Treasury Secretary Jack Lew reversed the plan, opting instead to replace Andrew Jackson with Harriet Tubman on the $20 bill; this decision was later reversed by the first Trump administration, with Harriet Tubman not being selected for either bill. On April 12, 2016, Miranda and Jeremy McCarter released Hamilton: The Revolution, detailing the musical's creation and including behind-the-scenes stories and footnotes from Miranda, which won the Goodreads Choice Award for Nonfiction in 2016 and the Audiobook of the Year at the Audie Awards in 2017. After premiering at the New York Film Festival on October 1, 2016, PBS's Great Performances aired the documentary Hamilton's America on October 21, 2016, directed by Alex Horwitz, which explored the show's creation with newly shot footage of the New York production, visits to Mount Vernon and Valley Forge, and interviews with historians, experts, politicians, and musicians, earning a 100% rating on Rotten Tomatoes. Hamilton: The Exhibition, an interactive museum focusing on Alexander Hamilton’s life and the musical, debuted in Chicago in April 2019 on Northerly Island, designed to travel and led by Jeffrey Seller, with David Korins as artistic designer and Joanne Freeman as historical consultant; Alex Lacamoire provided orchestration, and Lin-Manuel Miranda, actors, and historians delivered recorded presentations. The exhibition closed on August 25, 2019, and plans to relocate were cancelled, with refunds issued for tickets purchased from August 26 to September 8. Following Hurricane Maria, Lin-Manuel Miranda, with family roots in Vega Alta, Puerto Rico, used his influence to highlight Puerto Rico’s struggles and promote tourism; in 2017, he and his father, Luis Miranda Jr., opened the Placita Güisín, a café and restaurant in Vega Alta, which later became a tourist attraction after Miranda moved his memorabilia to a new gallery within it and opened a merchandise store, TeeRico. After a November 18, 2016 performance with Vice President-elect Mike Pence in the audience, Brandon Victor Dixon delivered a statement from the stage, jointly written by the cast, Miranda, and producer Jeffrey Seller, expressing concern about Pence’s new administration and its potential impact on American values, rights, and diversity; Pence stated he was not offended, but Trump demanded an apology for what he called harassment, leading to the #BoycottHamilton campaign, which was widely mocked despite the show being sold out months in advance. The Washington Post criticized Trump’s response as divisive, noting a racial and cultural divide in the 2016 election and suggesting he could have offered assurances of inclusivity; Robert Dallek described Trump’s Twitter reaction as a "striking act of divisiveness," with the Hamilton cast acting as a symbol of those fearing Trump’s policies. Jeffrey Seller stated that while Trump had not seen Hamilton or inquired about tickets, he was welcome to attend. In April 2016, Jeb! The Musical appeared online, replacing Alexander Hamilton with Jeb Bush and featuring political figures like Trump and Chris Christie in supporting roles, with the staged reading at Northwestern University prepared with the same rigor as Jeb’s campaign, crowdsourced by writers from Yale, Boston University, McGill, and the University of Michigan through a Facebook group called "Post Aesthetics." In 2016, Gerard Alessandrini created Spamilton, a revue parodying Hamilton and other Broadway shows, which premiered at the Triad Theater in New York and played at the Royal George Theatre in Chicago. On October 12, 2016, Modern Family aired an episode, "Weathering Heights," in which Manny records a parody of "Alexander Hamilton" as part of his college application, with most other applications also being parodies. In 2022, a Transformers: BotBots episode, "I, Cheeseburger," featured a musical parody of Hamilton with an identical poster and fast-food-themed versions of songs. "Weird Al" Yankovic released a polka medley of Hamilton songs in 2018 as part of the Hamildrops program and followed it in 2020 with a video using footage from the filmed version. In 2022, a church in Texas, The Door Christian Fellowship, produced an illegal version of Hamilton known as Scamilton, which was live-streamed to YouTube around August 22 and reuploaded on August 28. Ham4Progress, a group of Hamilton cast members and staff, supports social justice causes, including abortion rights through fundraising for The Brigid Alliance and Planned Parenthood, and trans rights through collaboration with the Trans Youth Equality Foundation. The group also supports environmental issues by partnering with NRDC. On February 3, 2021, Hamilton Families, with cast member Christopher Henry Young, spoke about addressing family homelessness in the SF Bay Area. In 2021, Ham4Progress hosted "The Joy In Our Voices," featuring Lin-Manuel Miranda, Senator Cory Booker, poet Amanda Gorman, Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock, Gayle King, and Hamilton performers, highlighting Black art and artists for Black History Month. Ham4Progress also recognized May as Asian & Pacific American Heritage Month, with director Jon M. Chu discussing AAPI representation with cast members Marcus Choi and Taeko McCaroll. Several original stage performances from the Richard Rodgers Theatre in 2016 were filmed by RadicalMedia and offered for bidding to major studios; on February 3, 2020, Walt Disney Studios acquired the distribution rights for $75 million, with an original theatrical release date of October 15, 2021, under Walt Disney Pictures. Miranda announced on May 12, 2020, that due to the pandemic’s impact on the film industry and performing arts, the film would be released early on Disney+ on July 3, 2020, for the Fourth of July weekend. The film was acclaimed for its visuals, performances, and direction, becoming one of the most-streamed films of 2020, and was named one of the best films of 2020 by the American Film Institute, nominated for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy and Best Actor in a Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy (for Miranda) at the 78th Golden Globe Awards, and Daveed Diggs was nominated for the Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Male Actor in a Limited Series or Television Movie. Hamilton received 12 nominations at the 73rd Primetime Emmy Awards, including Outstanding Lead Actor for Miranda and Odom Jr., Outstanding Supporting Actor for Groff, Ramos, and Diggs, and Outstanding Supporting Actress for Soo and Goldsberry. The film had a wide theatrical release in the United States and Canada on September 5, 2025, to celebrate the musical’s tenth anniversary, featuring new "Reuniting the Revolution" interviews with the original cast and creators, playing in 1,825 screens and grossing $10.1 million, ranking second at the box office behind The Conjuring: Last Rites. Further releases were scheduled in the United Kingdom and Ireland on September 26 and in Australia and New Zealand on November 13, 2025. On February 10, 2017, Miranda speculated that a film adaptation would eventually be made, but not for years to allow audiences to see the stage version first. On July 6, 2020, after the Disney+ release, Miranda stated he did not love many movie musicals based on stage shows because it was hard to "stick the landing," and he did not know what a cinematic version of Hamilton would look like, saying if he had, he would have written it as a movie. In December 2024, following the success of Universal Pictures' Wicked, interest in a screen adaptation of Hamilton grew again, with Miranda stating the property should wait at least "10 more years" due to the success of the live film recording, though he did say "if someone's got an idea, holla at me."
